name: Suspended Judgment

detectability.signature: A perfect ring of refracted starlight enclosing a disc of deep-field sky that belongs to somewhere else; exotic negative-mass readings along the rim

proximity: Compass references disagree by a few degrees as the throat's field brushes sensor range
Starlight through the aperture resolves into an unfamiliar sky
contact: Transit is smooth but absolute; vessels emerge 14,000 light-years away with clocks offset by 0.3 seconds
Unshielded electronics briefly forget their boot sequences on arrival
prolonged_exposure: Loitering in the throat causes progressive desynchronization of onboard chronometers
Repeated transits within one hour produce cumulative navigational error at the far mouth

phenomena: The ring's interior displays a fixed alien starfield regardless of observer position
The aperture visibly swells and contracts on its six-minute cycle without changing mass readings
Light from the far mouth arrives pre-bent, doubling images of the destination cluster
hazards: Navigation system failure if transited off-cycle during aperture minimum
Chronic desynchronization from normal spacetime for ships that linger in the throat
opportunities: Shortcut through normal space, spanning 14,000 light-years in a single transit
Access to otherwise unreachable regions beyond the Veil Drift
Strategic chokepoint control over all traffic to the far colonies
known_incidents: Discovery credit goes to the mining tug Anser's Luck, whose crew followed an anomalous parallax reading and emerged above a constellation no chart recognized
Toll wars were fought over the near mouth twice in the last century; both ended when whoever held the ring simply closed the lane to their rivals' hulls
description: Suspended Judgment hangs in empty space as a ring of polished darkness forty-five kilometers across, its rim bending the light of our own galaxy while its center holds a patient, unfamiliar sky. Sensors read negative mass density along the rim, a signature no natural object produces. The geometry is too clean, too deliberate, to be anything but built.

The aperture breathes on a six-minute cycle, swelling and subsiding with metronomic regularity, and transits are safest in the middle third of each breath. A crossing takes under a second and deposits a vessel fourteen thousand light-years away, its clocks lagging by less than a second. Whoever built it tuned the throat for stability; six centuries of use have not shifted its endpoints by a meter.

The tug Anser's Luck found it while chasing a parallax ghost, and the subsequent land rush established the far colonies that now depend entirely on this single door. Two toll conflicts confirmed what everyone already suspected: the side that controls the ring controls half a quadrant. Engineers have failed, politely and repeatedly, to determine who the builders were or why they abandoned it.

Traffic control stations orbit both mouths, running schedules keyed to the breathing cycle, and smugglers pay handsomely for off-cycle transit windows. Archaeological teams drift at a respectful distance, mapping construction seams in the rim that match nothing in any catalog. Every transit is a small act of trust in unknown engineers who left no other trace of themselves.
